planting.note: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in fall in gritty, well-drained soil where clumps can be left undisturbed to naturalize; foliage is boldly mottled and striped in maroon-purple.

directions: Plant bulbs 4–5 inches deep and 4–6 inches apart in fall in a sunny site with sharp drainage, leaving clumps undisturbed for years rather than lifting them annually like hybrid tulips. Greigii tulip is prized as much for its broad, wavy leaves boldly mottled and striped in maroon-purple as for its large, often scarlet-red flowers, which open wide in full sun to reveal a dark-blotched center on relatively short, sturdy stems that resist wind damage better than taller hybrid types. Native to the mountains of Central Asia, it tolerates heat and dry summers better than most modern hybrid tulips and is one of the most reliable species tulips for perennializing in the garden. Choose a site with excellent drainage, since like all tulips it is prone to bulb rot in soggy soil, especially through summer dormancy.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in fall in gritty, well-drained soil where clumps can be left undisturbed to naturalize; typically the earliest tulip species to flower each spring.

directions: Plant bulbs 4–5 inches deep and 4–6 inches apart in fall in a sunny site with sharp drainage, leaving clumps undisturbed to naturalize rather than lifting them annually like hybrid tulips. Waterlily tulip is typically the earliest tulip to bloom each spring, opening its slender, pointed buds into wide, flat flowers on sunny days — the flattened, multi-petaled look that gives the species its common name — usually in bicolor combinations of red, cream, and yellow, and closing again at night or in overcast weather. Native to the mountains of Central Asia, it is shorter and generally longer-lived in the garden than large hybrid tulips, spreading gradually into a low carpet of bloom well suited to rock gardens and the front of a sunny border. Give it excellent drainage, since like all tulips it is prone to bulb rot in soggy soil, especially through its summer dormancy.
